results.summary: This design converts a 4-bit binary input into a 7-segment display pattern using a simple combinational circuit of OR and AND gates. It is tested by setting the first four switches to a binary value from 0 to 15 and observing the display. No external hardware beyond the switches and a 7-segment display is required. Silicon testing confirmed correct operation for digits 0 through 9, but values 10 to 15 do not display, which the testers note may be intentional but would be nicer as hexadecimal.

This project blinks the letter A on a 7-segment display, with each output pin driving one segment plus the decimal point. The documentation consists only of placeholder text, so the internal logic and intended test procedure are not described. It needs only a 7-segment display connected to the eight outputs. A silicon test report confirms that it did blink an A, but the lack of documentation makes the design's details unclear.

This design generates pseudo-random bit streams whose probability of a one equals the product of two 2-bit input vectors, implementing stochastic multiplication based on a published PN-sequence method. It is used by setting inputs A and B, applying a clock, and toggling reset low to start the PRBS generators, with outputs providing the product stream and individual operand streams. No external hardware is strictly required, though some outputs are also mapped to 7-segment segments. The documentation is brief and cites the underlying paper, but does not describe the internal implementation or provide silicon test results.

This is a hardware implementation of two-player ping pong rendered on a 16x24 LED matrix, using up/down counters for each paddle and the ball plus an input register to debounce buttons. It requires substantial external hardware: a 16-bit serial-in parallel-out shift register, a 5-to-24 decoder, the LED matrix, eight buttons, BCD counters with 7-segment displays for scoring, and a timing unit to generate the enable and clock signals. Testing can start simply by hooking up left/right buttons for player one and monitoring the horizontal position bits, but full functionality needs the complete external support circuitry. The design is notable for its detailed pin-level documentation and its reliance on external multiplexing and decoding to drive the matrix.

This project is a simple ring oscillator that outputs a square wave on pins 0 through 3, with the pins phase shifted relative to one another. It is tested simply by applying power, with no other control inputs described. No external hardware is needed beyond observing the outputs. The documentation is very thin and does not specify the oscillation frequency or the exact phase relationship, so those details cannot be confirmed.

This project demonstrates one of each basic logic gate together with some flip-flops, intended as a gate-level playground. The documentation is placeholder text, so the exact circuit and test method are not described. It appears to use the eight outputs for 7-segment segments, but the connection to the logic is unclear. The author's silicon test report notes a 1 Hz clock while tracing the logic through the Wokwi diagram, and that momentary push-button mode helped separate gate tests from flip-flop tests.

This design combines a tapped ring oscillator with a glitchless clock source switch, allowing selection between two external clocks. To test the oscillator, one of the three inverted taps is fed back to input 0, while the clock switch is tested by using input 1 to select between clock0 and clock1, with the selected clock appearing on output 3. No external hardware beyond clock sources and feedback wiring is required. The documentation is concise but describes both functional blocks and their test procedure clearly.

This project is a Tiny Tapeout 5 workshop design whose first three output bits form a binary counter that can be preset with the first three input bits, while the remaining input bits pass through to the outputs. The documentation does not explain how to test it, leaving the test procedure unspecified. No external hardware is described, though the outputs are mapped to 7-segment segments. The design appears to be a teaching example from a workshop, but the sparse documentation limits what can be said about it.

This design divides the input clock by successive powers of two, with CLK/2 on output 7 down to CLK/256 on output 0. The documentation is placeholder text and does not describe the internal implementation or how to test it. It requires only a clock input and observation of the divided outputs, with no other external hardware mentioned. Because the documentation is essentially empty, the summary is inferred from the title and pin names.

This Verilog design generates a sawtooth waveform for audio by incrementing a counter from 0 to 25,000,000 and feeding the value into a PDM modulator, with the frequency set by a 4-bit left-shift amount. It is tested by adding an RC low-pass filter with a cutoff around 30 kHz to output pin 7, which can be probed with an oscilloscope or connected to an audio amplifier to listen to the result. The design outputs both PCM bits and a PDM stream, and follows the Tiny Tapeout audio pinout recommendation. It is notable for being a straightforward audio waveform generator that requires external filtering and amplification to be useful.
